risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down separately: the category result rests on 41,201 samples and is visible in the raw scatter (Fig 6A). Unstandardized methods across six laboratories and repeat submissions by the same producer add noise and dependence, and the cluster χ² and some effect sizes are unreliable (card sc_smith_2022, JBI moderate), but these weaken the secondary associations, which the statement words with their limits. The Dutch study is at high risk of bias (small unsystematic sample, post hoc exclusions, no tests, a conflict of interest; card sc_hazekamp_2012) and only qualifies the claim.

inconsistency.note: The Dutch study points the same way on variation within names, and on THC not telling its two cultivars apart; with two cultivars it cannot test the categories in general.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level: the categories tested are those a consumer website's database attaches to strain names, matched by name, not the labels printed on packages or given at sale; only terpenes were compared, not THC or CBD; the products are compliance-tested flower from six US states in 2013–2021; and nothing about effects was measured, although effects are what people usually mean by the labels.

imprecision.note: A very large sample for the category result; no intervals are printed, but the score sits near zero by a wide margin. The name results rest on 41 names and are given as counts.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one analysis of laboratory records; the cleaned data and code are stated to be public.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim: never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3).

rate.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read.
rate.population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
rate.exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
rate.comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
rate.outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured
rate.magnitude: Smith et al. (2022), THC-dominant samples with terpene results (n = 41,201): mean silhouette score −0.03 for the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (groups: Hybrid 17,616, no category 12,322, Indica 6,681, Sativa 4,582), 0.27 for the dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters; differences |d′| = 3.49 (k-means against category), 1.83 (dominant terpene against category) and 0.54 (k-means against dominant terpene), all P < 0.0001; no intervals. Clusters: I (caryophyllene-limonene) 21,811 (52.9%), II (myrcene-pinene) 14,188 (34.4%), III (terpinolene-myrcene) 5,202 (12.6%). Strain names (41): more consistent than shuffled names for 26, no different for 13, less consistent for 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) (editors' count of the Fig 8C significance marks; the text gives one test for the majority of names, P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed); shuffled baseline about 0.69 cosine similarity (read from Fig 8C); Purple Punch 96% of products in one cluster against 61.8% expected under shuffling, Tangie 62.5% in its most common cluster. Category shares among 12,063 products with a category (editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III Hybrid 55.8%, Indica 13.3%, Sativa 30.9% (χ² 22.2, P < 0.0001 as printed); editors' calculation: the χ² formula applied to the Fig 9B percentages as if they were counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III and 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, which the paper reports as not different. Hazekamp & Fischedick (2012): THC 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88) in Amnesia against 159.5 (SD 26.76) in White Widow, reported as not significantly different with no test shown; myrcene 0.7 against 2.9 mg/g; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia, not detected in White Widow; relative standard deviation above 25% for 14 compounds as printed (editors' count of Table 1: 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds); 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other cultivar.
rate.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
rate.rate: One very large set of lab records, but it checked only smell compounds, used a strain website's labels instead of the packages, and measured no effects on people.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_miller_1999 (RoB 2): some concerns (allocation concealment not described; no registered plan). Beyond those questions: family members and therapists knew the assignment; therapists were nested within approaches, with CRAFT's less experienced therapists supervised by its developer, a co-author, and the two main CRAFT therapists engaged 50% and 91% of their cases; two of the four pooled trials come from a team that includes CRAFT's developer and one tested its first version, and the review (card sc_roozen_2010: AMSTAR 2 critically low) reports only a summary quality score for each trial. Entry into treatment was largely recorded by the projects rather than rated by the family members. One level, not two: the difference is large, and every trial, including the two with no author in common with any other included trial (Sisson & Azrin, 1986; Kirby et al., 1999, as summarized by the review), points the same way.

inconsistency.note: I² 2.9%; all four trial estimates favour CRAFT (relative risks 2.34 to 9.75).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: treatment entry, the outcome measured, in families of adults who refused treatment, in US trials with trained and supervised therapists delivering about 12 hours of sessions. The statement says that drinking and drug use, safety, families living with violence and family members in less frequent contact are outside it.

imprecision.note: 224 family members and 102 treatment entries in the pooled comparison; the interval (2.11 to 5.02) excludes small effects. The comparison with the Johnson intervention (one trial of 85; 1.28 to 3.62) is less precise and is worded as resting on one trial.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review, and with four trials no test would be informative; the search left out trial registries and grey literature. The concern that small trials from the developers' groups dominate is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

rate.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias −1 (see the domain note), which gives moderate, for the statement that training family members in CRAFT, rather than in a twelve-step family approach, increases the share of relatives who enter treatment. Causal wording ('increases') fits the randomized design at this certainty. The comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on one trial and is worded as such; on its own it would be rated lower for imprecision. The statements about family members' own wellbeing describe what the trials found (no difference between approaches, improvement in all groups) and are not rated as an effect of any approach, since no trial had an untreated group; the review's within-group pooling cannot answer that question. The claim does not adopt the review's 'almost three times' for the Johnson comparison (its own result is a relative risk of 2.15), its suggestion that partner violence may also have fallen (no data, and the largest trial excluded families with recent violence), or its 'strong evidence' that the approaches improve family members' functioning. Status replicated: four trials point the same way; two of them (Sisson & Azrin, 1986; Kirby et al., 1999) share no author with any other included trial, and the other two share three authors, including CRAFT's developer.
rate.population: Family members (spouses, partners, parents and other relatives; 88–100% women across trials; aged 19 to 81) of adults with alcohol problems (two trials) or illicit drug use, cocaine most often (two trials), who refused treatment, in four US randomized trials published 1986–2002 (264 family members). In the largest trial, 130 family members in Albuquerque, New Mexico (91% women; 59% spouses, 30% parents; recruited mostly through local news media), living with the relative and seeing them on at least 40% of days; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe illicit drug problem were excluded
rate.exposure: CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training): in the largest trial up to 12 one-hour individual sessions (about 12 hours of therapist contact) teaching the family member to reward not drinking, communicate positively, plan competing activities, handle dangerous situations and suggest treatment; in the oldest trial its first version, community reinforcement training
rate.comparator: Twelve-step family approaches (Al-Anon facilitation therapy, an Al-Anon model or Nar-Anon) in all four trials; a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares family members for a group confrontation, in one trial; no untreated group in any trial
rate.outcome: The relative entering treatment (at least one session; in the largest trial an assessment and at least one session within 6 months); family members' own depression, anger, family cohesion and conflict, and relationship happiness
rate.magnitude: Miller et al. (1999), engaged within 6 months: CRAFT 29/45 (64%), Johnson 12/40 (30%), Al-Anon facilitation 6/45 (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001; CRAFT against Johnson χ²(1, N = 85) = 10.29, p < .001; Al-Anon facilitation against Johnson p < .06. Editors' calculation (Wald 95% intervals): CRAFT minus Johnson 34.4 percentage points (14.5 to 54.4); CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51.1 points (34.0 to 68.3). Within 12 months 67%, 35% and 20% (Table 1). Adjusted for drinking at intake, extra therapy and relationship type: Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002. Johnson group: 70% did not hold the confrontation; 9 of the 12 that did saw the relative enter treatment, against 3 of 28 within 6 months. Across groups, parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% against 32% at 6 months). Family members: no group-by-time interaction and no group effect; Beck Depression Inventory means 10.6–10.8 at intake and 7.0–7.5 at 6 months in all three groups. Roozen et al. (2010): CRAFT against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon, 4 trials, 84/125 (67%) against 18/99 (18%), RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), NNT 2, I² 2.9%; trial RRs 9.75 (0.67–141.44), 4.83 (2.22–10.50), 3.86 (1.28–11.64), 2.34 (1.31–4.16); without the smallest trial 3.21 (1.99–5.17); CRAFT against Johnson (one trial) RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), NNT 3; within CRAFT groups, baseline against 6 months, depression WMD 3.60 (0.99–6.22), 74 family members in two trials.
rate.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment within 6 months, against 30 and 13 with other approaches.
rate.rate: Families were assigned by chance, and the gap was big and pointed the same way in every trial. But there are only four small US trials, two of them from CRAFT's creators.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable: both are narrative reviews without selection criteria or appraisal (cards sc_lader_2011 and sc_brett_2015: high). The 15–30 in 100 figure is the author's own earlier review; the severe-reaction table rests on a guide and the author's monograph and is called mostly anecdotal; the 2015 review's seizure statements are unreferenced.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews agree that seizures can follow abrupt stopping; the 2015 review cites the 2011 one, so they are not independent.

indirectness.note: Second-hand throughout; the only seizure count comes from 11 prisoners on several times the usual dose in 1961, unlike stopping usual doses today or stopping after high-dose use outside medical care.

imprecision.note: No rate is given for seizures or any other severe reaction; the one count rests on 11 people.

rate.reasoning: Observational and anecdotal sources, seen only through two narrative reviews: starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which goes below the floor: very low. The claim rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither review gives how often seizures or other severe reactions follow sudden or gradual stopping, and neither cites a study comparing the two; this does not mean such reactions are rare or absent, and the statement says that both reviews describe them. Status single study: the only count of seizures comes from one 1961 study, described second-hand. No tapering schedules, amounts or timings are given, by design; the reviews' schedules and dose equivalents are not reproduced.
rate.population: People stopping or reducing regular benzodiazepine use (prescribed anxiolytics and sleeping pills, and high-dose use outside medical care), as described in two narrative reviews; in the one study with a seizure count (1961, as described), 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months
rate.exposure: Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly, or reducing or stopping them gradually, after regular use
rate.comparator: None in the sources described; neither review cites a study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping
rate.outcome: Withdrawal symptoms (how often, which, how long), rebound, and severe reactions including seizures, delirium, psychosis and suicidal thoughts
rate.magnitude: Not estimable for seizures or other severe reactions: neither review gives a frequency. As described: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients (Lader, 2011, citing Lader, 1998, ref. 124). 1961 study (Hollister et al., as described): 11 prisoners, chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months, switched to placebo; 10 had withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures. The seizure statements in Brett & Murnion (2015) carry no references.
rate.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
rate.rate: Two expert reviews, not new studies. Their figures are second-hand, the seizure warnings give no rates, and the only count comes from 11 prisoners on very high doses in 1961.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_hughes_2017 (RoB 2): high, for the outcome (stated intentions about hypothetical scenarios, answered by people who had just answered a contrasting scenario) and for selective reporting (no registration, half the survey reported, the stated significance threshold not applied, regression outcome inconsistent with the percentages, p values differing between text and table). A self-selected online sample recruited partly through drug forums.

indirectness.note: The claim concerns what people do at festivals; the study measured what they said they would do in written scenarios, in one Australian online sample in 2015, and collected but did not analyse amounts or drug types.

imprecision.note: 2,115 people; the differences in stated intentions are measured precisely, but they are not the outcome the claim is about.

rate.reasoning: Starts low: the main comparison, police against no police, is within person, with the order of the two scenarios not reported, so it is rated as observational; the outcome is a survey answer. Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 go below the floor: very low. The comparison between strategies was randomized between blocks, but would also be very low for the claim as worded (high, then risk of bias −1 and indirectness −2 for hypothetical intentions standing in for behaviour). Worded as insufficient evidence because no behaviour was measured; the percentages are reported as stated intentions of this sample, and the regression results and the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying are not adopted. Status single study: the same team's 2014 pilot, described in the paper, was not read.
rate.population: 2,115 people aged 18 or over living in Australia who had been to at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online in late 2015 mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (mean age 22.3; 54.9% men; 89.1% lifetime and 78.4% recent illicit drug use; 47.0% ever stopped by police); 506 to 561 per randomized block
rate.exposure: Written scenarios of policing at a 30,000-person outdoor festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside), riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police), three drug detection dogs at the gates, or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers)
rate.comparator: A written scenario with no police present, answered by the same people (order not reported); between strategies, the randomized blocks
rate.outcome: Stated intention (yes or no) to use illicit drugs, carry them into the grounds, buy them inside, give them to a friend inside or sell them inside; perceived likelihood of detection. Actual behaviour was not measured
rate.magnitude: Stated intentions, % (Table 4). Any police against no police: any offence 72.8 against 77.4 (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6 against 76.5 (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carry in 52.6 against 62.8 (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); buy inside 39.5 against 36.8 (+2.7; p = 0.001 in the text, < 0.001 in the table); give 26.9 against 28.9; sell 3.5 against 5.1 (p values differ between text and table). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 (p < 0.001); carry 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 (p = 0.711); any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 (p = 0.003, above the paper's own 0.001 threshold). Detection judged likely or very likely for use or possession: dogs 52.3%, riot 32.9%, high-visibility 26.5%, collaborative 14.9%, no police 1.8%. Last festival (self-report): 65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police. Regression odds ratios not used: editors' calculation from Table 4, odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing = (29.4/70.6)/(23.4/76.6) = 1.36 (of offending 0.73), against the printed 2.687.
rate.short: Not by much, going by what people said. With sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 said they'd still use drugs, against 77 with no police, in an Australian online survey.
rate.rate: One online survey of people who chose to take part, about made-up scenarios. What people say they'd do isn't always what they do, and some of the paper's statistics don't add up.

item.statement: Indica and sativa labels show which smell compounds a weed has.
item.why: In 41,201 US lab-tested samples, the labels barely matched the terpene mix. The labels came from a strain website, and effects weren't measured.

lines.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
lines.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed felt.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples that licensed growers sent for testing in six US states, 2013 to 2021. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name.
In 41,201 samples high in THC, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.

item.why: In one small Dutch study, a sativa-type and an indica-type coffee-shop strain had similar THC but different terpenes. That's two strains, not a rule.

item.statement: Confronting someone as a family works best to get them into treatment.
item.why: In one trial, 30 in 100 relatives started treatment after confrontation training, against 64 in 100 after CRAFT skills training. Seven in 10 families never held the confrontation.

lines.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment within 6 months, against 30 and 13 with other approaches.
lines.but: Just four small US trials, and two came from the team that created CRAFT.
how: The biggest trial had 130 family members, mostly women, living with someone with a drinking problem. Each got one of three approaches by chance, about 12 hours each.

Within 6 months, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment after CRAFT. It was 30 after training for a family confrontation, and 13 after counselling to join Al-Anon. Seven in 10 families chose not to hold the confrontation.
Pooling four trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, relatives started treatment about 3 times as often with CRAFT as with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches: 67 against 18 in 100.
Family members felt less depressed and angry after 6 months in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.

item.why: In one trial, family members felt less depressed and angry in every group, whether or not the relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.

item.statement: In a survey, most festival-goers said sniffer dogs would stop them using drugs.
item.why: With dogs, 66 in 100 still said they'd use drugs, against 77 with no police. These were answers to made-up scenarios, not real behaviour.

lines.short: Not by much, going by what people said. With sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 said they'd still use drugs, against 77 with no police, in an Australian online survey.
lines.but: It's what people said they'd do at a made-up festival, not what they really did.
how: 2,115 Australian festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, took an online survey. Each read about a made-up festival with no police, and one with police, riot police, sniffer dogs or police working with health workers.
With any police, 70 in 100 said they'd use drugs and 53 in 100 that they'd carry drugs in, against 77 and 63 with no police. With sniffer dogs, 47 in 100 said they'd carry drugs in.
Slightly more said they'd buy drugs inside the festival when police were there: 40 against 37 in 100. The authors worry those drugs may not be what they're sold as, which wasn't checked.
Police working with health services made almost no difference: 75 in 100 still said they'd use drugs. The survey didn't ask how much people would take.

item.statement: Benzo withdrawal can feel like the anxiety or sleep problems the pills were for.
item.why: Both reviews say withdrawal symptoms can resemble the original problem. They are expert reviews, so this is second-hand.

lines.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
lines.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one cites no source at all.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound. They can feel like the problem the pills were for, and sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep even after a few nights.
Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen with slow tapering, but calls most reports anecdotes; the other cites no source.
The only count: in 1961, 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

item.statement: Reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos say how often they happen.
item.why: Both reviews read warn of seizures, but neither gives a rate. The only count is 2 of 11 prisoners in 1961, in conditions unlike usual use.

lines.statement: In dried cannabis flower that licensed growers sent for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in six US states (Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington; December 2013 to January 2021; 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results), the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category that one consumer cannabis website's strain database links to each strain name, matched by name to the growers' own sample names (so the category is the website's, not necessarily what each package said; 73.4% of samples could be given one), was barely related to the samples' terpene profiles, the mix of the compounds the authors describe as responsible for cannabis's smell (Smith et al., 2022). THC and CBD content were not compared between the categories, and no effects on people were measured. In the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results, a score of how much more samples resemble others with the same label than samples with the nearest other label (the silhouette score, from −1 to 1) averaged −0.03 for the categories, with most samples below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their most abundant terpene and 0.38 for three groups found by a clustering method in the same terpene data, which the authors expected to separate better; the category analysis also counted 12,322 samples (29.9%) that had no category as a group of their own. Strain names carried more information: for 26 of the 41 names attached to at least five growers with at least five samples each, products sold under the same name by different growers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random, 13 did not differ from chance and 2 (LSD and Durban Poison) were less alike than chance (editors' count of the significance marks in the paper's figure); even randomly paired products were fairly similar, at about 0.69 on a 0-to-1 similarity scale (read from the figure). Among 12,063 THC-dominant products with a category, Sativa products made up 30.9% of the terpinolene-rich group against 15.0% overall, yet that group was still mostly Hybrid (55.8%), and the test the paper reports for this appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts (editors' calculation). The six laboratories' methods were not standardized, which the authors say prevents them from separating laboratory from regional differences, and the corresponding author is employed by the website that supplied the categories and strain names. In a small Dutch study, two cultivars that a seed company's website describes as Sativa-dominant (Amnesia) and Indica-dominant (White Widow), bought at ten coffee shops in four cities on two visits about two months apart (35 samples), differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but had similar THC (about 17% and 16% of the weight); many compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases of the same name, 3 samples had the chemistry of the other cultivar and were left out as presumed mix-ups, and of three pharmacy varieties one, bred from a variety with a large share of Sativa genes, resembled the Indica-dominant cultivar (Hazekamp & Fischedick, 2012; no statistical tests of these differences; the first author worked for the grower of the pharmacy varieties). Neither study measured how the products felt, so neither can say whether the labels predict effects. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
lines.exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
lines.comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
lines.outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured
lines.magnitude: Smith et al. (2022), THC-dominant samples with terpene results (n = 41,201): mean silhouette score −0.03 for the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (groups: Hybrid 17,616, no category 12,322, Indica 6,681, Sativa 4,582), 0.27 for the dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters; differences |d′| = 3.49 (k-means against category), 1.83 (dominant terpene against category) and 0.54 (k-means against dominant terpene), all P < 0.0001; no intervals. Clusters: I (caryophyllene-limonene) 21,811 (52.9%), II (myrcene-pinene) 14,188 (34.4%), III (terpinolene-myrcene) 5,202 (12.6%). Strain names (41): more consistent than shuffled names for 26, no different for 13, less consistent for 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) (editors' count of the Fig 8C significance marks; the text gives one test for the majority of names, P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed); shuffled baseline about 0.69 cosine similarity (read from Fig 8C); Purple Punch 96% of products in one cluster against 61.8% expected under shuffling, Tangie 62.5% in its most common cluster. Category shares among 12,063 products with a category (editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III Hybrid 55.8%, Indica 13.3%, Sativa 30.9% (χ² 22.2, P < 0.0001 as printed); editors' calculation: the χ² formula applied to the Fig 9B percentages as if they were counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III and 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, which the paper reports as not different. Hazekamp & Fischedick (2012): THC 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88) in Amnesia against 159.5 (SD 26.76) in White Widow, reported as not significantly different with no test shown; myrcene 0.7 against 2.9 mg/g; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia, not detected in White Widow; relative standard deviation above 25% for 14 compounds as printed (editors' count of Table 1: 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds); 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other cultivar.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read.

lines.q: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed?
lines.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
lines.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed felt.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples that licensed growers sent for testing in six US states, 2013 to 2021. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name.
In 41,201 samples high in THC, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.

lines.statement: In family members (mostly women: spouses, partners and parents) of adults with alcohol or other drug problems who refused treatment, training the family member in CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training; in the largest trial about 12 hours of individual sessions with a therapist, teaching ways to reward not drinking, to communicate, to handle dangerous situations and to suggest treatment) compared with twelve-step family approaches increases the share of relatives who enter treatment, in four small US randomized trials published 1986–2002, two of them by a team that includes CRAFT's developer and one testing its first version. In the largest trial (130 family members in Albuquerque, USA, 91% women, living with a relative with a drinking problem and seeing them on at least 40% of days; Miller et al., 1999), the relative entered treatment within 6 months (at least an assessment and one session) in 29 of 45 cases (64 in 100) after CRAFT, 12 of 40 (30 in 100) after a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares the family for a group confrontation, and 6 of 45 (13 in 100) after Al-Anon facilitation, up to 12 individual sessions encouraging involvement in Al-Anon, which the authors note is not the same as a simple referral to Al-Anon; in the Johnson group, 70 in 100 families chose not to hold the confrontation, and 9 of the 12 that did saw their relative enter treatment. Across the four trials (two on alcohol, two on illicit drugs, cocaine most often), relatives entered treatment in 84 of 125 CRAFT cases (67 in 100) against 18 of 99 with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches (18 in 100): relative risk 3.25 (95% CI 2.11 to 5.02), with every trial pointing the same way (I² 2.9%; Roozen et al., 2010); the comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on the one trial (relative risk 2.15, 1.28 to 3.62), which the review's discussion calls almost three times as effective. Family members' own depression, anger and family relationships improved over 6 months by similar amounts in all three groups of the largest trial, whether or not the relative entered treatment; with no group left without help, no approach can be credited with that improvement, and the review's pooled 'improvement' compares scores before and after within the CRAFT groups only. The trials counted whether the relative started treatment, not drinking or drug use, which the largest trial reports separately (not read here), or safety; the largest trial excluded families where the relative had been violent in the past 2 years, had a history of severe violence or had a drug problem worse than the drinking, and families with any sign of crack cocaine or injecting drug use; family members and therapists knew which approach they had; therapists were not crossed with approaches (in the largest trial, CRAFT's less experienced therapists were supervised by the approach's developer, a co-author); and the review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 on its study card (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no trial-by-trial risk-of-bias judgments, no check for unpublished trials). Certainty: moderate, for treatment entry against twelve-step family approaches. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Family members (spouses, partners, parents and other relatives; 88–100% women across trials; aged 19 to 81) of adults with alcohol problems (two trials) or illicit drug use, cocaine most often (two trials), who refused treatment, in four US randomized trials published 1986–2002 (264 family members). In the largest trial, 130 family members in Albuquerque, New Mexico (91% women; 59% spouses, 30% parents; recruited mostly through local news media), living with the relative and seeing them on at least 40% of days; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe illicit drug problem were excluded
lines.exposure: CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training): in the largest trial up to 12 one-hour individual sessions (about 12 hours of therapist contact) teaching the family member to reward not drinking, communicate positively, plan competing activities, handle dangerous situations and suggest treatment; in the oldest trial its first version, community reinforcement training
lines.comparator: Twelve-step family approaches (Al-Anon facilitation therapy, an Al-Anon model or Nar-Anon) in all four trials; a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares family members for a group confrontation, in one trial; no untreated group in any trial
lines.outcome: The relative entering treatment (at least one session; in the largest trial an assessment and at least one session within 6 months); family members' own depression, anger, family cohesion and conflict, and relationship happiness
lines.magnitude: Miller et al. (1999), engaged within 6 months: CRAFT 29/45 (64%), Johnson 12/40 (30%), Al-Anon facilitation 6/45 (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001; CRAFT against Johnson χ²(1, N = 85) = 10.29, p < .001; Al-Anon facilitation against Johnson p < .06. Editors' calculation (Wald 95% intervals): CRAFT minus Johnson 34.4 percentage points (14.5 to 54.4); CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51.1 points (34.0 to 68.3). Within 12 months 67%, 35% and 20% (Table 1). Adjusted for drinking at intake, extra therapy and relationship type: Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002. Johnson group: 70% did not hold the confrontation; 9 of the 12 that did saw the relative enter treatment, against 3 of 28 within 6 months. Across groups, parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% against 32% at 6 months). Family members: no group-by-time interaction and no group effect; Beck Depression Inventory means 10.6–10.8 at intake and 7.0–7.5 at 6 months in all three groups. Roozen et al. (2010): CRAFT against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon, 4 trials, 84/125 (67%) against 18/99 (18%), RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), NNT 2, I² 2.9%; trial RRs 9.75 (0.67–141.44), 4.83 (2.22–10.50), 3.86 (1.28–11.64), 2.34 (1.31–4.16); without the smallest trial 3.21 (1.99–5.17); CRAFT against Johnson (one trial) RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), NNT 3; within CRAFT groups, baseline against 6 months, depression WMD 3.60 (0.99–6.22), 74 family members in two trials.
lines.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias −1 (see the domain note), which gives moderate, for the statement that training family members in CRAFT, rather than in a twelve-step family approach, increases the share of relatives who enter treatment. Causal wording ('increases') fits the randomized design at this certainty. The comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on one trial and is worded as such; on its own it would be rated lower for imprecision. The statements about family members' own wellbeing describe what the trials found (no difference between approaches, improvement in all groups) and are not rated as an effect of any approach, since no trial had an untreated group; the review's within-group pooling cannot answer that question. The claim does not adopt the review's 'almost three times' for the Johnson comparison (its own result is a relative risk of 2.15), its suggestion that partner violence may also have fallen (no data, and the largest trial excluded families with recent violence), or its 'strong evidence' that the approaches improve family members' functioning. Status replicated: four trials point the same way; two of them (Sisson & Azrin, 1986; Kirby et al., 1999) share no author with any other included trial, and the other two share three authors, including CRAFT's developer.

lines.q: How can I get a family member who refuses help into treatment?
lines.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment within 6 months, against 30 and 13 with other approaches.
lines.but: Just four small US trials, and two came from the team that created CRAFT.
how: The biggest trial had 130 family members, mostly women, living with someone with a drinking problem. Each got one of three approaches by chance, about 12 hours each.

Within 6 months, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment after CRAFT. It was 30 after training for a family confrontation, and 13 after counselling to join Al-Anon. Seven in 10 families chose not to hold the confrontation.
Pooling four trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, relatives started treatment about 3 times as often with CRAFT as with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches: 67 against 18 in 100.
Family members felt less depressed and angry after 6 months in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say how often stopping benzodiazepines suddenly leads to seizures or other severe withdrawal reactions, or how much stopping gradually lowers that risk. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews (Lader, 2011, a descriptive review based on a lecture; Brett & Murnion, 2015, a four-page clinical review for prescribers that cites the 2011 review elsewhere), stopping or cutting down after regular use can bring a withdrawal syndrome: the 2011 review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use but only in about 15 to 30 in 100 patients, a figure cited to the author's own 1998 paper on stopping sleeping pills, and that rebound (the original symptoms returning more strongly for a while) is likely when stopping sleeping pills, especially short-acting ones, even after a few nights of use; the 2015 review states, without a reference, that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly. Symptoms listed include anxiety and panic, poor sleep and nightmares, poor memory and concentration, low mood, muscle spasms and aches, numbness and tingling, sweating, and heightened sensitivity to light, sound and touch, with feelings of unreality; the 2011 review says they generally fade within weeks or months, often fluctuating, and both reviews say they can resemble the anxiety or insomnia the drug was taken for. Both reviews describe seizures. The 2011 review lists convulsions (which, it says, may end in death), delirium, psychosis, depression, often severe, and suicidal thoughts among reactions that may follow abrupt stopping but may also occur despite slow tapering, with no frequencies, in a table sourced mainly to a university guide and the author's 1984 monograph (the depression entry to a report of four cases), says many of them are reported anecdotally, with few case series, and that their status remains controversial; it adds that whether withdrawal occurs is related to high doses and long treatment but its severity less closely, and that severe withdrawal may occur despite withdrawal over months or years. The 2015 review states, without a reference or a frequency, that abrupt stopping after 1 to 6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, lists grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping in a box without a source, and describes people without a history of seizures, unstable medical or psychiatric illness or other drug dependence as at lower risk of harm from withdrawal, also without references. The only count of seizures in either review comes from a 1961 study in which 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months were switched to a dummy pill: within 2 to 8 days, 10 developed withdrawal reactions, including depression, psychosis and agitation, and 2 had seizures. Neither review cites a study comparing sudden with gradual stopping for seizures; the 2011 review says the rate at which doses are reduced rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good evidence, and that, in high-dose use as in low-dose dependence, withdrawal can sometimes be severe, with fits and psychotic reactions. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People stopping or reducing regular benzodiazepine use (prescribed anxiolytics and sleeping pills, and high-dose use outside medical care), as described in two narrative reviews; in the one study with a seizure count (1961, as described), 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months
lines.exposure: Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly, or reducing or stopping them gradually, after regular use
lines.comparator: None in the sources described; neither review cites a study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping
lines.outcome: Withdrawal symptoms (how often, which, how long), rebound, and severe reactions including seizures, delirium, psychosis and suicidal thoughts
lines.magnitude: Not estimable for seizures or other severe reactions: neither review gives a frequency. As described: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients (Lader, 2011, citing Lader, 1998, ref. 124). 1961 study (Hollister et al., as described): 11 prisoners, chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months, switched to placebo; 10 had withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures. The seizure statements in Brett & Murnion (2015) carry no references.
lines.reasoning: Observational and anecdotal sources, seen only through two narrative reviews: starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which goes below the floor: very low. The claim rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither review gives how often seizures or other severe reactions follow sudden or gradual stopping, and neither cites a study comparing the two; this does not mean such reactions are rare or absent, and the statement says that both reviews describe them. Status single study: the only count of seizures comes from one 1961 study, described second-hand. No tapering schedules, amounts or timings are given, by design; the reviews' schedules and dose equivalents are not reproduced.

lines.q: Is it dangerous to stop benzos suddenly?
lines.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
lines.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one cites no source at all.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound. They can feel like the problem the pills were for, and sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep even after a few nights.
Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen with slow tapering, but calls most reports anecdotes; the other cites no source.
The only count: in 1961, 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether police or drug detection ('sniffer') dogs at outdoor music festivals change whether people use, carry, buy or supply drugs there: the one study read measured what people said they would do in written scenarios, not what they did (Hughes et al., 2017). In a national online survey in late 2015 of 2,115 Australians aged 18 or over who had been to an outdoor music festival in the past year (mean age 22; recruited mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media; 89 in 100 had ever used an illicit drug and 78 in 100 recently), each person was assigned at random, by block, to two scenarios for a festival of 30,000 people; by the paper's paired analysis, one with no police and one of four policing scenarios: high-visibility policing (over 200 police), riot policing (over 400, including riot squads and mounted police), three sniffer dogs at the gates, or police working with health services. With any police, 72.8 in 100 said they would commit some drug offence, against 77.4 in 100 with no police; 69.6 against 76.5 said they would use drugs and 52.6 against 62.8 that they would carry drugs into the grounds, while 39.5 against 36.8 said they would buy drugs inside the grounds; stated giving and selling fell slightly (26.9 against 28.9; 3.5 against 5.1). With sniffer dogs, 66.3 in 100 said they would use drugs and 47.1 that they would carry them in; with police working with health services, 75.1 and 59.4, close to no police. Under high-visibility policing, riot policing and sniffer dogs, about two in three said they would use drugs (66.3 to 69.2 in 100), close to the 65.3 in 100 who said they had used drugs at their last festival. The strategies did not differ significantly in stated buying (43.8 in 100 with dogs; p = 0.711), so the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying is not supported by its own test. The paper set significance at 0.001 but treats larger p values as significant, prints test results for giving and selling that differ between its text and table, and reports regression results whose outcome does not match its percentages (by the editors' calculation, the odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing are about 1.36, not the printed 2.69), so only the percentages are used here. The order of the two scenarios is not reported; the sample chose to take part, so the figures describe it, not festival-goers in general; and drug types and amounts were collected but not analysed, so the study says nothing about how much people would take, or about the hurried taking of drugs to avoid detection, a concern the paper cites from other sources. The authors suggest that buying inside the grounds could raise the risk of taking adulterated or mislabelled drugs, which the survey did not measure. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 2,115 people aged 18 or over living in Australia who had been to at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online in late 2015 mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (mean age 22.3; 54.9% men; 89.1% lifetime and 78.4% recent illicit drug use; 47.0% ever stopped by police); 506 to 561 per randomized block
lines.exposure: Written scenarios of policing at a 30,000-person outdoor festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside), riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police), three drug detection dogs at the gates, or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers)
lines.comparator: A written scenario with no police present, answered by the same people (order not reported); between strategies, the randomized blocks
lines.outcome: Stated intention (yes or no) to use illicit drugs, carry them into the grounds, buy them inside, give them to a friend inside or sell them inside; perceived likelihood of detection. Actual behaviour was not measured
lines.magnitude: Stated intentions, % (Table 4). Any police against no police: any offence 72.8 against 77.4 (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6 against 76.5 (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carry in 52.6 against 62.8 (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); buy inside 39.5 against 36.8 (+2.7; p = 0.001 in the text, < 0.001 in the table); give 26.9 against 28.9; sell 3.5 against 5.1 (p values differ between text and table). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 (p < 0.001); carry 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 (p = 0.711); any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 (p = 0.003, above the paper's own 0.001 threshold). Detection judged likely or very likely for use or possession: dogs 52.3%, riot 32.9%, high-visibility 26.5%, collaborative 14.9%, no police 1.8%. Last festival (self-report): 65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police. Regression odds ratios not used: editors' calculation from Table 4, odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing = (29.4/70.6)/(23.4/76.6) = 1.36 (of offending 0.73), against the printed 2.687.
lines.reasoning: Starts low: the main comparison, police against no police, is within person, with the order of the two scenarios not reported, so it is rated as observational; the outcome is a survey answer. Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 go below the floor: very low. The comparison between strategies was randomized between blocks, but would also be very low for the claim as worded (high, then risk of bias −1 and indirectness −2 for hypothetical intentions standing in for behaviour). Worded as insufficient evidence because no behaviour was measured; the percentages are reported as stated intentions of this sample, and the regression results and the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying are not adopted. Status single study: the same team's 2014 pilot, described in the paper, was not read.

lines.q: Do police and sniffer dogs at festivals stop people taking drugs?
lines.short: Not by much, going by what people said. With sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 said they'd still use drugs, against 77 with no police, in an Australian online survey.
lines.but: It's what people said they'd do at a made-up festival, not what they really did.
how: 2,115 Australian festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, took an online survey. Each read about a made-up festival with no police, and one with police, riot police, sniffer dogs or police working with health workers.
With any police, 70 in 100 said they'd use drugs and 53 in 100 that they'd carry drugs in, against 77 and 63 with no police. With sniffer dogs, 47 in 100 said they'd carry drugs in.
Slightly more said they'd buy drugs inside the festival when police were there: 40 against 37 in 100. The authors worry those drugs may not be what they're sold as, which wasn't checked.
Police working with health services made almost no difference: 75 in 100 still said they'd use drugs. The survey didn't ask how much people would take.
